rows.question: When does my maternity leave start if my due date is 15 November 2026?
rows.reply:
Under the Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) rules, the period before the birth covers the last six weeks before the delivery. MuSchG §3(1) says an employer may not employ a pregnant woman "in den letzten sechs Wochen vor der Entbindung" (the Schutzfrist vor der Entbindung), unless she expressly declares that she is willing to work. She can withdraw that declaration at any time, with effect for the future.

The start is counted from the expected date of delivery as shown on the certificate from a doctor, a midwife or an Entbindungspfleger ("der voraussichtliche Tag der Entbindung … wie er sich aus dem ärztlichen Zeugnis … ergibt"). If your certificate gives 15 November 2026, the period before the birth is the six weeks before that date. The excerpts do not set out how the individual days of those six weeks are counted, so they do not fix the exact first day. Your employer, who is the one barred from employing you, can be asked to confirm the date they are working from.

If the baby is not born on the expected day, the period before the birth becomes shorter or longer to match (MuSchG §3(1)).

After the birth, the protection period runs until eight weeks after delivery. It is extended to twelve weeks in three cases: 1. premature births (Frühgeburten), 2. multiple births (Mehrlingsgeburten), and 3. where a disability of the child is medically established before the eight weeks end. Case 3 applies only if the mother applies for it. If the baby arrives early, the period after the birth is also extended by the time the period before the birth was cut short (MuSchG §3(2)). The Familienportal confirms that with twins or more, the period before the birth also starts six weeks before the expected date, as with one child.

MuSchG §15 says a pregnant woman should tell her employer about the pregnancy and the expected date of delivery as soon as she knows, and should show a doctor's or midwife's certificate if the employer asks. For Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity benefit) from a statutory health insurer, the same certificate stating the expected delivery date governs payment before the birth (SGB V §24i(3)).

The Familienportal notes that self-employed women are not covered by the Mutterschutzgesetz.

rows.question: How long after birth can we apply for Elterngeld without losing money?
rows.reply:
The law does not set an application deadline. It limits how far back payment goes. Under BEEG §7(1), Elterngeld (parental allowance) must be applied for in writing ("Elterngeld ist schriftlich zu beantragen"). It is then paid retroactively only for the last three Lebensmonate before the start of the Lebensmonat in which the application was received: "rückwirkend nur für die letzten drei Lebensmonate vor Beginn des Lebensmonats geleistet, in dem der Antrag auf Elterngeld eingegangen ist." Earlier months than that are not paid.

This matters because, under BEEG §4(1), Elterngeld can be drawn from the day of birth ("Es kann ab dem Tag der Geburt bezogen werden"). An application received later than this three-month look-back loses those earliest months of payment.

The excerpts do not define how a Lebensmonat is counted. Your Elterngeldstelle decides Elterngeld applications, so that is where to ask how this applies to your child's dates.

rows.question: How much notice do I have to give my employer for Elternzeit?
rows.reply:
Elternzeit (parental leave (unpaid job-protected leave)) is requested from your employer, not from an authority. BEEG §16(1) sets the minimum notice by when the leave falls.

- For leave up to the child's third birthday, you must request it at the latest seven weeks before it begins ("spätestens sieben Wochen").
- For leave between the third birthday and the eighth birthday, you must request it at the latest 13 weeks before it begins ("spätestens 13 Wochen").

The request must be made "in Textform". The Familienportal explains that this means a letter without a signature or an email is also possible.

If you request leave under the first case, up to the third birthday, you must also state at the same time which periods within two years you will take as Elternzeit. For a mother whose Elternzeit follows the maternity protection period, that period counts towards the two years. If it follows annual leave taken after the maternity protection period, both the maternity protection period and the annual leave count.

Shorter notice is possible only as an exception. Where there are urgent reasons, an appropriate shorter period is possible ("Bei dringenden Gründen ist ausnahmsweise eine angemessene kürzere Frist möglich"). The Familienportal gives premature births and an adoption placement that could not be planned in time as examples. It also says no general period can be stated for these cases, because it depends on the circumstances of the individual case.

Separately, under BEEG §16(2), a mother who cannot request Elternzeit in time for leave that follows directly on from the maternity protection period, for a reason she is not responsible for, may make the request within one week after that reason ends.

The Familienportal also states that for births before 1 July 2015 the notice period is seven weeks in every case, including leave after the third birthday. The statutory transitional provision behind this is not among the excerpts here. Your employer applies the notice rules, and BEEG §16(1) requires the employer to certify your Elternzeit to you.

Related: under BEEG §18(1), your employer may not dismiss you from the point at which you requested Elternzeit. That protection begins at the earliest eight weeks before leave up to the third birthday, and at the earliest 14 weeks before leave between the third and eighth birthdays.

rows.question: How long is maternity protection after the birth if the baby comes early?
rows.reply:
The answer depends on whether the early birth counts as a Frühgeburt (premature birth) in the legal sense, or is simply earlier than the expected date.

The basic rule. After the birth, the employer may not employ the mother until eight weeks have passed: "bis zum Ablauf von acht Wochen nach der Entbindung" (MuSchG §3(2)). This is the Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) after the birth.

Extension to twelve weeks. The period after the birth is extended to twelve weeks in three cases (MuSchG §3(2)):
1. "bei Frühgeburten" (premature births),
2. "bei Mehrlingsgeburten" (multiple births),
3. where, before eight weeks after the birth have passed, a disability within the meaning of SGB IX §2(1) is medically established in the child. This third extension applies only if the mother applies for it ("nur, wenn die Frau dies beantragt"). The official guidance page says this application is made to the health insurance fund (Krankenkasse).

The twelve-week extension does not apply to a stillbirth ("Satz 2 gilt nicht bei einer Totgeburt").

Added days for any early birth. Before the birth, the protection period runs for the last six weeks before the expected date, and it is shortened if the baby arrives before that date (MuSchG §3(1)). When the birth is early, the period after the birth is extended by the amount by which the period before the birth was shortened. This applies to both the eight-week and the twelve-week period: "Bei vorzeitiger Entbindung verlängert sich die Schutzfrist nach der Entbindung nach Satz 1 oder nach Satz 2 um den Zeitraum der Verkürzung" (MuSchG §3(2)).

The federal guidance page puts it this way. If the baby is born before the expected date but is not a premature birth, the protection period still totals 14 weeks. It ends later than eight weeks after the birth by as many days as the baby was early. If the baby counts medically as a premature birth, protection runs 12 weeks after the birth. The page gives as an example a birth weight under 2,500 grams. The statute excerpt itself does not define "Frühgeburt". The page also states that there are no special statutory protection periods after a caesarean section.

After the birth, the mother may not work during this period even if she wants to. The exception in the excerpts is for school and university students, who may resume their studies if they expressly ask their place of education. If an employer nonetheless asks her to work, the guidance page says she can turn to her supervisory authority (Aufsichtsbehörde).

rows.question: Can my employer dismiss me while I am pregnant?
rows.reply:
In general, no. Kündigungsschutz (protection against dismissal) under MuSchG §17(1) makes a dismissal "unzulässig" (not permitted) in three periods:
1. during pregnancy;
2. until four months after a miscarriage after the twelfth week of pregnancy;
3. until the end of the protection period after the birth, and at least until four months after the birth.

The protection applies if the employer knows of the pregnancy, miscarriage or birth when dismissing, or is told "innerhalb von zwei Wochen nach Zugang der Kündigung" (within two weeks of receiving the dismissal). Missing those two weeks does no harm if the reason was not your fault and you inform the employer without delay. The same rules apply to steps the employer takes to prepare a dismissal (MuSchG §17(1)). Familienportal adds that the protection also applies if you did not yet know you were pregnant, but you must already have been pregnant when the dismissal was received.

There is one exception. Under MuSchG §17(2), the state's highest authority for occupational safety, or a body it designates, may "ausnahmsweise" (exceptionally) declare a dismissal permissible. This is only possible in special cases not connected with the woman's condition during pregnancy, after a miscarriage or after the birth. Such a dismissal must be in writing and must state the reason. Familienportal gives examples of such reasons: insolvency, partial closure of the business, a small business that cannot continue without a qualified replacement, or a particularly serious breach of duty. The employer must apply in writing to the supervisory authority (Aufsichtsbehörde). Without its approval, the dismissal is ineffective.

If you are dismissed without that approval, Familienportal says you must bring a claim before the labour court (Arbeitsgericht). It says the claim is "normalerweise innerhalb von 3 Wochen" (normally within 3 weeks) of receiving the written dismissal. If no claim is brought, the dismissal is treated as effective. You can bring the claim yourself, through a lawyer, or orally at the court office. Familienportal also says you should involve the supervisory authority.

If the authority approved the dismissal, you can challenge that approval. Depending on the Bundesland, this is done by objection (Widerspruch) or by a court claim. This is a separate procedure and does not replace the claim before the labour court.

If you take Elternzeit after the birth, the protection can be extended (BEEG §18). On a fixed-term contract, maternity protection ends when the contract ends.

Whether a particular dismissal is permissible is decided by the supervisory authority and, in a dispute, by the labour court. The supervisory authority is responsible for compliance with the Mutterschutzgesetz, so you can take questions about your own situation there.

rows.question: Is there an income limit above which we get no Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes. Under BEEG §1(8), the claim to Elterngeld (parental allowance) lapses ("Ein Anspruch entfällt") if the person entitled had zu versteuerndes Einkommen (taxable income) of more than 175,000 euros in "dem letzten abgeschlossenen Veranlagungszeitraum vor der Geburt des Kindes". Taxable income here means taxable income as defined in § 2 Absatz 5 of the Einkommensteuergesetz.

Whose income counts depends on who else qualifies. If another person also meets the conditions in §1(1) sentence 1 number 2 (living in one household with the child), or in §1(3) or §1(4), the claim lapses when the two people's taxable incomes added together exceed 175,000 euros. Otherwise the 175,000 euro limit applies to the entitled person's own taxable income.

The federal Familienportal makes two further points. Taxable income is not the same as gross income, which is usually considerably higher. Your individual taxable income is determined by the Finanzamt and appears in the Steuerbescheid, which should be attached to the Elterngeld application where it exists. The portal also describes different, higher limits for earlier births. The statutory excerpts here do not include the transitional rules for those births, so they do not settle which limit governs a particular birth.

If the Steuerbescheid for the last completed Veranlagungszeitraum before the birth is not yet available, you can still apply. BEEG §8(2) provides that if, on the information in the application, the limit is not expected to be exceeded, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation in case it turns out to have been exceeded. BEEG §8(3) provides that the amount is then decided provisionally until the required information is supplied.

Whether the limit applies to your family is decided only by the Elterngeldstelle for your district. That office handles your application, so it is where to ask about your own case.

rows.question: How many months of Elterngeld can we get in total?
rows.reply:
The total is not one number. It depends on which form of Elterngeld (parental allowance) you take and, for some births, on how early the child was born. Here is what the law provides for everyone.

Elterngeld is paid in Monatsbeträge (monthly amounts) for the child's Lebensmonate (BEEG §4(2)). According to the federal family portal, Lebensmonate are not calendar months. They start from the day of birth: for a child born on 15 February, the first Lebensmonat runs from 15 February to 14 March.

Basiselterngeld
- Parents together have a claim to twelve Monatsbeträge Basiselterngeld ("zwölf Monatsbeträge Basiselterngeld", BEEG §4(3)).
- They have a claim to two further months, the Partnermonate, if one parent's income from work is reduced in two Lebensmonate (BEEG §4(3)). That makes 14 months to share.
- One parent can receive at most twelve Monatsbeträge Basiselterngeld, plus up to four Monatsbeträge Partnerschaftsbonus under §4b (BEEG §4(4)).
- Each parent who claims must take Elterngeld for at least two Lebensmonate (BEEG §4(4)).
- Basiselterngeld can be received until the child completes the 14th Lebensmonat (BEEG §4(1)).

Elterngeld Plus
- Instead of one Lebensmonat of Basiselterngeld, a parent can take two Lebensmonate of Elterngeld Plus (BEEG §4(3)).
- Elterngeld Plus can be received until the child completes the 32nd Lebensmonat. From the 15th Lebensmonat onward, at least one parent must take it in consecutive Lebensmonate (BEEG §4(1)). The family portal adds that if both parents go without Elterngeld Plus for any Lebensmonat after the 14th, no more can be received afterwards, even if months remain.

Partnerschaftsbonus
- The statute refers to up to four Monatsbeträge Partnerschaftsbonus per parent under §4b (BEEG §4(4)).
- The family portal states that each parent can receive up to 4 additional months of Elterngeld Plus as Partnerschaftsbonus if both work part-time at the same time. §4b itself is not among these sources.

Premature births
Instead of the twelve months in §4(3), the parents' joint claim to Basiselterngeld is higher for a child born early (BEEG §4(5)):
1. at least six weeks before the expected delivery date: 13 Monatsbeträge;
2. at least eight weeks before: 14 Monatsbeträge;
3. at least twelve weeks before: 15 Monatsbeträge;
4. at least 16 weeks before: 16 Monatsbeträge.

In these four cases the limits change as well:
- The per-parent limit rises to 13, 14, 15 or 16 Monatsbeträge Basiselterngeld respectively, plus up to four Monatsbeträge Partnerschaftsbonus.
- Basiselterngeld can be received until the 15th, 16th, 17th or 18th Lebensmonat.
- Elterngeld Plus can still be received until the 32nd Lebensmonat. It must be taken in consecutive Lebensmonate from the 16th, 17th, 18th or 19th Lebensmonat respectively.
- The expected delivery date that counts is the one in the doctor's or midwife's certificate (BEEG §4(5)).

Months that count as already used
Lebensmonate in which a parent is entitled to certain benefits that are offset under §3(1) sentence 1 nos. 1 to 3 count as months of Basiselterngeld for that parent (BEEG §4(4)). The family portal explains that this covers months in which the mother receives Mutterschaftsgeld or other maternity benefits, whether or not Basiselterngeld is applied for.

Adopted children
For adopted children, Elterngeld can be received from when the child is taken in, at the latest until the child's eighth birthday (BEEG §4(1)).

These are the limits the law sets. How many months your family actually receives, and in which combination, is decided by the Elterngeldstelle on your application. Your district's Elterngeldstelle is the place to ask about your own case.

rows.question: What is the Partnerschaftsbonus and who qualifies?
rows.reply:
The Partnerschaftsbonus (partnership bonus months) is extra Elterngeld Plus for parents who both work part time at the same time. Under BEEG §4b(1), each parent gets an additional monthly amount of Elterngeld Plus for each Lebensmonat in which both parents work "nicht weniger als 24 und nicht mehr als 32 Wochenstunden im Durchschnitt des Lebensmonats" and both meet the conditions of BEEG §1. The excerpts do not set out what §1 requires.

The statute adds these limits:
- Each parent can receive at most four monthly amounts of Partnerschaftsbonus, and only if it is taken for at least two Lebensmonate (§4b(2)).
- Both parents must take it at the same time and in consecutive Lebensmonate (§4b(3)).
- If, while it is being paid, the conditions of §4c(1) no. 1 to 3 arise, one parent can continue it alone under §4c(2) (§4b(4)).
- The consecutive-months requirement still counts as met if it later turns out the conditions were not met in every month applied for (§4b(5)).

Averaging matters. The Familienportal page says you do not need 24 to 32 hours in every single week, only on average over the month. If you work more or less than planned, you must report it to your Elterngeldstelle. If either parent works under 24 or over 32 hours in a month, both lose the Partnerschaftsbonus for that month and it must be repaid. The other months are not affected as long as the conditions were met in at least 2 months.

One parent alone. Under BEEG §4c(2), a parent can get these additional Elterngeld Plus amounts alone if they work 24 to 32 weekly hours on average in two to four consecutive Lebensmonate and one of these grounds applies (§4c(1)):
1. the parent meets the conditions for the single-parent tax relief under §24b(1) and (3) of the Einkommensteuergesetz, and the other parent lives neither with them nor with the child;
2. care by the other parent would endanger the child's welfare within the meaning of §1666(1) and (2) BGB; or
3. care by the other parent is impossible, in particular because of serious illness or severe disability. Economic reasons and being busy with other activities do not count.

The Familienportal page also says separated parents can receive it. It can be used before, between or after the other Elterngeld months, even if you otherwise receive only Basiselterngeld. It is calculated the same way as Elterngeld Plus. The page states it is between 150 and 900 euros a month per parent, depending on income before the birth. That figure comes from a guidance page, and the excerpt carries no check date.

The page explaining part-time work describes the rules for children born after August 2021. For children born before 1 September 2021, partly different rules apply, and that page directs you to your Elterngeldstelle.

Whether you qualify, and for how many months, is decided by your Elterngeldstelle, so that is where to ask about your own case.

rows.question: We forgot to apply for Kindergeld. How far back will they pay?
rows.reply:
Kindergeld (child benefit) is paid retroactively for at most six months. The statute says payment of Kindergeld that has been set is made retroactively "nur für die letzten sechs Monate vor Beginn des Monats, in dem der Antrag auf Kindergeld eingegangen ist": only for the last six months before the start of the month in which the application was received. Months earlier than that are not paid out.

The same provision adds that the entitlement itself "bleibt von dieser Auszahlungsbeschränkung unberührt". The six-month limit restricts payment, not the entitlement.

The official family portal describes the same six months. It says this applies where Kindergeld was due to you but not paid, for example because no application was made. It also says to state in the application that you are applying retroactively, and from when you want Kindergeld.

The application must be made in writing. It should be made to the Familienkasse responsible under BKGG §13, which the portal describes as the Familienkasse at your Agentur für Arbeit. Because the payout limit counts back from the month the application is received, each month without one moves the earliest payable month forward.

The Familienkassen set Kindergeld by formal decision (Bescheid). Whether you were entitled, and for which months, is decided by your Familienkasse, not here, so that is where to ask about your own case. The portal gives the Bundesagentur für Arbeit's free service number for application questions: 0800 4 555530.

rows.question: How much Kindergeld do we get per month for our first child?
rows.reply:
Kindergeld (child benefit) is set by statute at 259 euros per month for each child. The law states: "Das Kindergeld beträgt monatlich für jedes Kind 259 Euro" (EStG §66(1); the same wording is in BKGG §6(1)). Because the amount is the same "für jedes Kind", the statute does not set a different figure for a first child. The excerpts do not give the date this figure was checked.

Kindergeld is paid monthly from the beginning of the month in which the conditions for entitlement are met, until the end of the month in which they cease (EStG §66(2)). If the tax allowances for children (Freibeträge für Kinder) are raised, Kindergeld is raised accordingly and rounded to full euros (EStG §66(3)).

During the year, parents first receive Kindergeld. In the annual income tax assessment, the Finanzamt then checks automatically whether the allowances for children or the Kindergeld paid is more favourable for the parents. This check does not need to be applied for.

This is the amount the law sets. It is not a decision on whether your family is entitled. That is decided by the Familienkasse, the authority the official guidance shows checking Kindergeld conditions, so that is where to ask about your own case. The official family portal links to the online Kindergeld application with the Bundesagentur für Arbeit.

rows.question: How quickly do we have to register the birth at the Standesamt?
rows.reply:
The birth must be reported to the Standesamt (civil registry office) for the district where the child was born within one week. The statute says the birth is to be reported there "binnen einer Woche" (PStG §18(1)).

Under the same provision, the report is made in one of two ways:
1. by the persons named in §19 of the Personenstandsgesetz, orally or in writing, or
2. by the institutions named in §20 of the Personenstandsgesetz, in writing.

Persons reporting under the first route must substantiate the birth ("die Geburt des Kindes glaubhaft zu machen"). For a stillborn child, the report must be made at the latest on the third working day after the birth ("spätestens am dritten auf die Geburt folgenden Werktag").

The federal family portal says that if your child is born in a hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic, the facility notifies the responsible Standesamt and sends it the birth certificate from the birth (Geburtsbescheinigung). If your child is born at home, the midwife or doctor issues that certificate, and you must present it to the responsible Standesamt within one week.

The portal's checklist phrases the period as "innerhalb von 7 Werktagen" (within 7 working days). The statute says one week, and the statute is the legal source.

The excerpts do not say what happens if the report is late. For that, and for which further documents your Standesamt asks for, contact the Standesamt for the place of birth.

The Standesamt (civil registry office) for the place where your child is born. rows.question: What do we need to bring to the Standesamt to register the birth?
rows.reply:
The Standesamt (civil registry office) responsible for the child's place of birth is where you register the birth (Familienportal). The federal regulation PStV §33 lists the documents the Standesamt "soll verlangen" (should ask to see) when a birth is reported:

1. If the parents are married to each other: their marriage certificate ("Eheurkunde") or a certified extract from the marriage register ("beglaubigter Ausdruck aus dem Eheregister"). Also each parent's birth certificate, if the parents' birth registration details do not appear on the marriage certificate. The marriage certificate must be shown even if the marriage has ended.
2. If the parents are not married to each other: the mother's birth certificate. If paternity has already been acknowledged, also the declarations of acknowledgement, the father's birth certificate and, where they exist, the declarations of joint custody ("Sorgeerklärungen").
3. An identity card, passport or other recognised passport substitute for the parents ("Personalausweis, Reisepass oder ein anderes anerkanntes Passersatzpapier").
4. If the birth is reported in person ("bei mündlicher Anzeige"): a certificate of the birth issued by the doctor, midwife or male midwife who was present at the birth.

PStV §33 also says the Standesamt "kann die Vorlage weiterer Urkunden verlangen" (may ask for further documents) where they are needed to prove the details given.

On the birth certificate from the doctor or midwife (the "Geburtsbescheinigung"), Familienportal says:
- If the child was born in a hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic, that institution notifies the responsible Standesamt and sends it the Geburtsbescheinigung.
- If the child was born at home, the midwife or doctor issues the Geburtsbescheinigung, and you must present it to the responsible Standesamt within one week.

If both parents are foreign nationals, PStV §34(1) adds a further requirement. When the birth is reported, the Standesamt asks for information on whether a parent holds an unlimited right of residence ("unbefristetes Aufenthaltsrecht"), or a residence permit under the EU–Switzerland free movement agreement as a Swiss national or their family member. This is to check whether the child acquired German citizenship by birth under StAG §4(3). The Standesamt then asks the Ausländerbehörde to confirm the details in writing. It also makes this request if the parents give no details or it doubts them (PStV §34(2)). The Standesamt makes the decision on citizenship (PStV §34(3)).

Familienportal says the further documents needed are listed on the website of the Standesamt in the place where your child is born. That Standesamt is the place to check the full list for your registration.

rows.question: Does my Krankenkasse pay for a midwife?
rows.reply:
Yes, the statutory health insurance law gives this right. Under SGB V §24d, an insured woman has a right to midwife help ("Hebammenhilfe") during pregnancy, at the birth and after the birth. This includes the examinations to establish the pregnancy and prenatal check-ups ("Untersuchungen zur Feststellung der Schwangerschaft und zur Schwangerenvorsorge").

There is one time limit on postnatal care. The right to Hebammenhilfe for care after the birth ("Wochenbettbetreuung") runs until the end of twelve weeks after the birth ("bis zum Ablauf von zwölf Wochen nach der Geburt"). Further services after that need a doctor's order ("bedürfen der ärztlichen Anordnung").

If the mother cannot look after the child after the birth, the insured child has its own right to the midwife services that relate to the child.

The Familienportal puts it the same way: every woman with statutory health insurance has a right to support from a Hebamme (midwife). If you are privately insured, it says you should check with your insurer beforehand which services it covers.

The excerpts do not describe how to arrange or claim midwife care. Whether this applies to you depends on your own insurance. Your Krankenkasse (statutory health insurer) is the place to ask about your own case.

rows.question: How do we insure the baby after the birth?
rows.reply:
Under SGB V §10, the children of members of statutory health insurance are insured through Familienversicherung (family cover for dependants under statutory insurance). A child is covered under this rule if the child:
1. has their residence or habitual abode in Germany ("Wohnsitz oder gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt im Inland"),
2. is not insured in their own right under § 5(1) nos. 1 to 8, 11 to 12, and is not voluntarily insured,
3. is not exempt from insurance and not released from the insurance obligation,
4. is not self-employed as a main occupation, and
5. has no total income that regularly exceeds one seventh of the monthly reference figure under § 18 of SGB IV ("ein Siebtel der monatlichen Bezugsgröße").

Children are covered up to their 18th birthday. The statute extends this to age 23 if they are not in work, and to age 25 if they are in education or training or a voluntary service year. There is no age limit for children with disabilities who cannot support themselves (SGB V §10(2)).

There is one exclusion that matters for a newborn. The child is not insured this way if the parent who is married to or in a civil partnership with the member, and who is related to the child, meets all three of these conditions (SGB V §10(3)):
- they are not a member of a Krankenkasse,
- their total income regularly exceeds one twelfth of the annual earnings limit ("ein Zwölftel der Jahresarbeitsentgeltgrenze") per month, and
- their income is regularly higher than the member's.

If the conditions are met through more than one parent, the member chooses the Krankenkasse (§10(5)).

The member must report the people insured under Familienversicherung to the responsible Krankenkasse, with the details needed to carry out the cover. Any later changes to those details must also be reported (§10(6)). The national association of health insurance funds sets a uniform procedure and uniform forms for this report.

The Familienportal lists registration with the Krankenkasse as one of the things you need the child's birth certificate for. You must register the child within 1 week at the Standesamt for the place of birth, and the Standesamt issues the birth certificate. If the child was born in a hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic, that facility notifies the Standesamt. In many maternity clinics, Lotsendienste explain benefits and help with filling in applications, free of charge.

The excerpts do not cover how a child is insured if neither parent is in statutory health insurance, and they set no time limit for the report to the Krankenkasse. Whether your child meets these conditions is not something this service can assess. The responsible Krankenkasse receives the report under §10(6), and that is where to ask about your own child.

rows.question: When are the first check-ups for the baby?
rows.reply:
The Kinder-Richtlinie (children's guideline) of the Gemeinsamer Bundesausschuss sets out ten check-ups in the first six years of life, U1 to U9 (including U7a). It says they "können nur in den jeweils angegebenen Zeiträumen unter Berücksichtigung folgender Toleranzgrenzen in Anspruch genommen werden". That means each check-up can only be used within its stated period or its tolerance window.

The first check-ups:
- U1: "unmittelbar nach der Geburt" (immediately after birth). It should be done within the first 30 minutes after the birth. If no doctor is present at the birth but a midwife is, the midwife should carry it out. U1 has no tolerance window.
- U2: 3rd to 10th day of life ("3.-10. Lebenstag"). Tolerance window: 3rd to 14th day.
- U3: 4th to 5th week of life ("4.-5. Lebenswoche"). Tolerance window: 3rd to 8th week.
- U4: 3rd to 4th month of life ("3.-4. Lebensmonat"). Tolerance window: 2nd to 4½th month.
- U5: 6th to 7th month. Tolerance window: 5th to 8th month.
- U6: 10th to 12th month. Tolerance window: 9th to 14th month.

The later check-ups are:
- U7: 21st to 24th month (tolerance 20th to 27th).
- U7a: 34th to 36th month (tolerance 33rd to 38th).
- U8: 46th to 48th month (tolerance 43rd to 50th).
- U9: 60th to 64th month (tolerance 58th to 66th).

For premature babies the same periods apply: "Auch bei Frühgeborenen sind die Untersuchungszeiträume einzuhalten." The prematurity is taken into account when the results are assessed.

The G-BA's page for the guideline notes that the version it offers does not yet include a decision that came into force on 20 August 2026.

The Bundeszentrale für gesundheitliche Aufklärung (BzGA) sends parent letters by email, timed to each upcoming check-up. They explain which documents to bring.

rows.question: What is Mutterschaftsgeld and when do I apply for it?
rows.reply:
What it is: Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is a payment for the protection periods before and after the birth and for the day of birth itself (MuSchG §19; SGB V §24i(3)). The excerpts do not give these periods in statutory form. The Familienportal guidance says the maternity protection periods "beginnen normalerweise 6 Wochen vor dem errechneten Geburtstermin und enden 8 Wochen nach der Geburt" (normally begin 6 weeks before the calculated due date and end 8 weeks after the birth).

There are two routes, depending on health insurance.

Members of a statutory health insurer receive Mutterschaftsgeld under SGB V (MuSchG §19(1)). Under SGB V §24i(1), it covers:
- female members who are entitled to sickness benefit when unable to work;
- female members who are not paid wages because of the protection periods;
- women whose employment ends immediately before the protection period begins, if they were insurance members on the last day of employment.

For members who are employed when the pre-birth protection period begins, the amount is the average net daily pay of the last three settled calendar months before that period, capped at "höchstens 13 Euro für den Kalendertag" (at most 13 euros per calendar day). Other members receive it at the level of sickness benefit (SGB V §24i(2)).

Where pay is above 13 euros a day, the employer pays a top-up. It is the difference between 13 euros and the average net daily pay of the last three settled calendar months before the protection period (MuSchG §20(1)). If employment ends by a dismissal under MuSchG §17(2), or the employer is insolvent, the body responsible for paying Mutterschaftsgeld pays the top-up instead (MuSchG §20(3)).

The entitlement rests while you receive pay, income or holiday compensation that is subject to contributions. One-off payments are the exception (SGB V §24i(4)).

Women who are not members of a statutory health insurer receive Mutterschaftsgeld paid by the federal government, "insgesamt höchstens 210 Euro" (at most 210 euros in total). It is paid "auf Antrag" (on application) by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung (Federal Office for Social Security) (MuSchG §19(2)).

When to apply: the excerpts do not set an application deadline or say when to apply. They state one requirement for payment before the birth. It depends on a certificate from a doctor or midwife that states the expected day of delivery (SGB V §24i(3)). If you are not in statutory health insurance, the application goes to the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung (MuSchG §19(2)). If you are a statutory member, the excerpts do not describe how or when to apply. Your statutory health insurer, which pays this benefit, is the place to ask.

Related: Mutterschaftsgeld under SGB V and the employer top-up are counted against Elterngeld. The 210-euro payment under MuSchG §19(2) is not (BEEG §3(1) No. 1).

rows.question: We are not married. Is my partner automatically the legal father?
rows.reply:
No. Under BGB §1592, the father of a child is the man who (1) is married to the child's mother at the time of the birth, (2) has acknowledged paternity ("die Vaterschaft anerkannt hat"), or (3) whose paternity has been established by a court under §1600d BGB or §182(1) of the Family Proceedings Act (FamFG). Being the mother's partner is not on that list.

If you are not married at the time of the birth, your partner must make a Vaterschaftsanerkennung (acknowledgement of paternity) to count legally as the father. It is voluntary and needs the mother's consent.

What BGB §1594 says about it:
- It can be made before the child is born (§1594(4)).
- It is not effective while another man's paternity exists (§1594(2)). For example, if the mother is married to another man at the birth, that husband is the legal father and an acknowledgement cannot be made. There is an exception where a divorce application was filed before the birth.
- An acknowledgement made subject to a condition or a time limit is invalid (§1594(3)).
- Its legal effects can generally be relied on only from the moment it becomes effective (§1594(1)).

Where it is made: your partner must make the declaration in person at a competent office, for example the Jugendamt, a Standesamt, an Amtsgericht or a notary. The mother must also give her consent in person. The office records both. Depending on the Bundesland, this can cost a fee at a notary or the Amtsgericht.

rows.question: How do unmarried parents get joint custody?
rows.reply:
If the parents are not married to each other when the child is born, the mother has parental custody (BGB §1626a(3): "Im Übrigen hat die Mutter die elterliche Sorge").

Under BGB §1626a(1), unmarried parents have joint custody in three cases:
1. they declare that they want to take on custody jointly, a Sorgeerklärung (declaration of joint custody);
2. they marry each other; or
3. the Familiengericht transfers custody to them jointly.

The father must first be legally recognised as the father. According to the Familienportal, this happens when he acknowledges the child as his own with the mother's consent, or when a court establishes paternity. Acknowledging paternity does not by itself give the father custody. A Sorgeerklärung or a court decision is also needed.

Sorgeerklärungen. Both parents make these declarations. The Familienportal says they can be made, for example, at the Jugendamt or before a notary, and can be made before the birth. When Sorgeerklärungen under BGB §1626a(1) No. 1 are made, an entry is made in the Sorgeregister kept at the competent Jugendamt (SGB VIII §58(1)).

Marriage. If the parents marry after the birth, they have joint custody.

Court transfer. On the application of one parent, the Familiengericht transfers custody, or part of it, to both parents jointly if this does not run counter to the child's welfare (BGB §1626a(2)). If the other parent puts forward no reasons against joint custody, and none are otherwise apparent, it is presumed that joint custody does not run counter to the child's welfare. The Familienportal adds that such reasons must be raised within a period set by the Familiengericht. In that case, the court decides in a simplified procedure, without hearing the Jugendamt and without a personal hearing of the parents. A court decision transferring custody jointly is also entered in the Sorgeregister once it is final (SGB VIII §58(1) No. 2).

Advice. Unmarried mothers and fathers have a right to advice on making a Sorgeerklärung and on the possibility of a court transfer of joint custody (SGB VIII §18(2)). The Familienportal says your local Jugendamt advises on all questions of parental custody, so that is where to ask about your own situation.

rows.question: Where do we apply for Elterngeld in Berlin?
rows.reply:
Elterngeld (parental allowance) is applied for at the Elterngeldstelle (the state office that decides parental allowance) responsible for your district. Under federal law, each Land designates the authorities that carry out the Elterngeld law. The responsible one is the authority "des Bezirks, in dem das Kind … zum Zeitpunkt der ersten Antragstellung seinen inländischen Wohnsitz hat": the district where the child lives when the first application is made (BEEG §12(1)). The excerpts do not name the individual Berlin offices, so check the Service Berlin page for Elterngeld for the office that covers your district.

The application must be made in writing ("schriftlich zu beantragen", BEEG §7(1)). It is signed by the parent who applies. The other entitled parent also signs to confirm they have seen it. This does not apply in the case of §4c or where one parent has sole custody (BEEG §7(3)).

There are two ways to apply in Berlin:

- Online through Service Berlin. You log in with a BundID account, or register for one if you do not have it. To log in with the "Online-Ausweis" option you need an electronic ID card, Unionsbürgerkarte or electronic residence permit (eAT) with the online ID function activated and its six-digit PIN. You also need a card reader or a modern Android or iOS smartphone, plus the AusweisApp software. Alternatively you can log in with an Elster certificate or with a username and password (Service Berlin).
- With ElterngeldDigital. This digital assistant helps you fill in the application in Berlin, Brandenburg, Bremen, Hamburg, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Niedersachsen, Rheinland-Pfalz, Sachsen-Anhalt, Schleswig-Holstein and Thüringen. You then print the document, sign it and post it to your responsible Elterngeldstelle. For technical problems or questions about the application, the ElternDigital support hotline is 0421 - 361 94195, Monday to Thursday, 10-12 and 13-15 (Familienportal).

Timing matters. Elterngeld is paid retroactively only for the last three Lebensmonate before the start of the Lebensmonat in which the application is received ("rückwirkend nur für die letzten drei Lebensmonate", BEEG §7(1)). Earlier months are not paid.

If something changes after you have applied, such as the payment period or bank details, Berlin asks you to use the Berlin Änderungsantrag (change application) for Elterngeld (Service Berlin).

Whether you qualify, and how much you receive, is decided by your Elterngeldstelle. That office is where to ask about your own case.

rows.question: Can we apply for Elterngeld online?
rows.reply:
Yes. The official family portal says Elterngeld (parental allowance) can be applied for digitally in every Bundesland: "Es gibt in allen Bundesländern die Möglichkeit, Elterngeld digital zu beantragen." You can also apply in person at an Elterngeldstelle. The application goes to the Elterngeldstelle responsible for your child's place of residence.

ElterngeldDigital (the federal online assistant for parental allowance applications) covers ten states: Berlin, Brandenburg, Bremen, Hamburg, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Niedersachsen, Rheinland-Pfalz, Sachsen-Anhalt, Schleswig-Holstein and Thüringen. Six states have their own online application, separate from ElterngeldDigital: Baden-Württemberg, Bayern, Hessen, Nordrhein-Westfalen, Saarland and Sachsen. For that, ask the Elterngeldstelle responsible for your child's place of residence.

What the law requires of the application, whichever route you use:

- It must be made in writing: "Elterngeld ist schriftlich zu beantragen" (BEEG §7(1)).
- Payment is backdated only for the last three Lebensmonate before the start of the Lebensmonat in which the application was received (BEEG §7(1)). Earlier months are not paid. The Elterngeldstelle decides on the application.

rows.question: Will our baby automatically be German if we are both Indian citizens?
rows.reply:
Not automatically because of your nationality. German law sets two routes to German Staatsangehörigkeit (citizenship) at birth, and parents' Indian citizenship does not trigger either one by itself.

Route 1, through a German parent. A child acquires German Staatsangehörigkeit by birth if a parent holds it (StAG §4(1)). If neither of you is German, this route does not apply.

Route 2, through birth in Germany to foreign parents. A child of foreign parents born in Germany ("durch die Geburt im Inland") acquires German Staatsangehörigkeit if one parent meets both of these conditions (StAG §4(3)):
1. that parent has had their lawful habitual residence in Germany for five years ("seit fünf Jahren rechtmäßig seinen gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt im Inland"), and
2. that parent holds an unlimited right of residence ("ein unbefristetes Aufenthaltsrecht"), or, as a Swiss national or a Swiss national's family member, a residence permit under the 1999 EC–Switzerland agreement on free movement.
Both conditions must be met by the same parent. Where the child acquires citizenship this way, it is entered in the Geburtenregister in which the birth is recorded.

How it is checked. When the birth is registered, the Standesamt asks whether a parent holds an unlimited right of residence. If the answers indicate that condition is met, the Standesamt obtains written information from the Ausländerbehörde on whether the answers are correct and whether that parent had five years' lawful habitual residence in Germany at the time of the birth. It also obtains this information, for both parents, if you give no details or it doubts them. The Standesamt then examines whether the child acquired German Staatsangehörigkeit and records the result (PStV §34(1)–(3)).

Whether your child meets these conditions is not something this service can assess. The Standesamt registering the birth makes that examination, so that is where to ask about your child's case.

If the child does not become German. A child born in Germany may be granted a residence permit (Aufenthaltserlaubnis) on the authorities' own initiative if one parent holds an Aufenthaltserlaubnis, a Niederlassungserlaubnis or an Erlaubnis zum Daueraufenthalt – EU. If both parents hold one of these at the time of birth, the child is granted the residence permit on the authorities' own initiative. If a parent holds a visa or may stay visa-free at the time of birth, the child's stay counts as permitted until that visa or visa-free stay ends (AufenthG §33).

The excerpts do not cover Indian citizenship law or whether your child also holds Indian citizenship.

rows.question: Does our newborn need a residence permit?
rows.reply:
Federal law attaches different rules depending on the parents' status at the time of birth. Whether your child needs an Aufenthaltserlaubnis (residence permit) is decided by the authorities, not here.

Residence permit for a child born in Germany (AufenthG §33):
- Both parents, or the parent with sole custody, hold an Aufenthaltserlaubnis, a Niederlassungserlaubnis or an Erlaubnis zum Daueraufenthalt – EU at the time of birth: the child is granted an Aufenthaltserlaubnis "von Amts wegen" (ex officio). The law says it "wird ... erteilt" (is granted).
- Only one parent holds one of these: the child "kann" (may) be granted an Aufenthaltserlaubnis ex officio. This is discretionary, not automatic.
- A parent holds a visa, or may stay without one, at the time of birth: the child's stay "gilt ... als erlaubt" (counts as permitted) until that visa or visa-free stay expires.

German citizenship by birth (StAG §4):
- A child acquires German citizenship at birth if one parent is German (§4(1)).
- A child of foreign parents born in Germany acquires it if one parent meets both conditions (§4(3)):
 1. has had lawful habitual residence in Germany for five years ("seit fünf Jahren rechtmäßig seinen gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt im Inland"), and
 2. holds an unlimited right of residence ("unbefristetes Aufenthaltsrecht"), or a residence permit under the EU–Switzerland free movement agreement as a Swiss national or their family member.
- If acquired, it is entered in the Geburtenregister (birth register) where the birth is recorded.

How citizenship is checked (PStV §34):
- When the birth is registered, the Standesamt asks whether a parent has an unlimited right of residence or the Swiss-agreement permit.
- It obtains written information from the Ausländerbehörde on whether this is correct and whether the parent had five years' lawful habitual residence at the time of birth. It also does this if the parents give no details or it doubts them. In that case, both parents are checked.
- The Standesamt then decides whether the child acquired German citizenship and records the result.

The excerpts do not say what a German citizenship finding means for the residence permit question. They also do not say which office issues the child's Aufenthaltserlaubnis or how. For your own child, ask your local Ausländerbehörde about the residence permit. For citizenship, ask the Standesamt where the birth is registered, which makes that check.

rows.question: We are getting Mutterschaftsgeld. Does that reduce our Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes. Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is counted against Elterngeld (parental allowance). BEEG §3(1) says it is "angerechnet" (offset) against the Elterngeld of the person entitled.

What is counted, under BEEG §3(1) No. 1, is maternity benefit due for the time from the day of the child's birth onward, in two forms:
- a) Mutterschaftsgeld under the Fünftes Buch Sozialgesetzbuch or the Zweites Gesetz über die Krankenversicherung der Landwirte. It is capped at "insgesamt höchstens 210 Euro" and paid by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung.

rows.question: Can I work while receiving Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes. Working part-time does not by itself end Elterngeld (parental allowance), but there is an hours limit, and income from work reduces the amount.

The hours limit. One condition of entitlement is that you work not at all or not full-time ("keine oder keine volle Erwerbstätigkeit", BEEG §1(1) no. 4). The law says a person is not working full-time if:
1. their working time does not exceed 32 hours a week on average over the Lebensmonat ("32 Wochenstunden im Durchschnitt des Lebensmonats");
2. they are in employment for vocational training ("Beschäftigung zur Berufsbildung"); or
3. they work as a qualified childminder within the meaning of §§23 and 43 of Book VIII of the Social Code (BEEG §1(6)).
People who are temporarily not working still count as working while they are in an employment relationship or are self-employed (BEEG §1(6a)).

How income affects the amount. For months after the birth in which your income from work is on average lower than before the birth, Elterngeld is paid at the applicable percentage of the difference between the two incomes. For this calculation, pre-birth income is counted up to at most 2,770 euros. The difference is calculated separately for months of Basiselterngeld and months of Elterngeld Plus (BEEG §2(3)). The maximum of 1,800 euros a month applies to full months in which you have no income from work (BEEG §2(1)). Instead of one month of Basiselterngeld, you can take two months of Elterngeld Plus (BEEG §4(3)). The federal family portal notes that Elterngeld Plus and, where both parents work part-time at the same time, the Partnerschaftsbonus can be of particular interest to parents working part-time.

What the application involves. If you state expected income from work in the application, you must prove your actual income for that period after the payment period ends (BEEG §8(1)), and the amount is decided provisionally until then (BEEG §8(3) no. 3). If you state that you expect no income from work, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation in case you do have income from work (BEEG §8(2)). The family portal says employees provide a certificate from their employer of their working hours during the payment period, and self-employed people provide their own declaration of past and current working hours.

The family portal says its explanations cover children born after August 2021, and that partly different rules apply for children born before 1 September 2021.

Whether your own hours and income fit these rules, and how much you would receive, is decided by your Elterngeldstelle. That is where to ask about your own case.

rows.question: Based on our situation, will our Elterngeld application be approved?
rows.reply:
Whether your application will be approved is a decision on your individual case. This service cannot assess or predict it. Only your Elterngeld office (Elterngeldstelle) decides, so that is where to ask about your own case.

What the law provides for everyone:

Under BEEG §1(1), Elterngeld (parental allowance) is available to a person who:
1. has a residence or habitual abode in Germany,
2. lives in one household with the child,
3. cares for and raises the child themselves, and
4. works not at all or not fully.

Under BEEG §1(6), a person is not fully employed if, among other cases, their working time does not exceed 32 hours a week on average over the Lebensmonat ("32 Wochenstunden im Durchschnitt des Lebensmonats").

Under BEEG §1(7), a foreign national without EU free-movement rights qualifies only with certain residence titles. These include:
- a Niederlassungserlaubnis or Erlaubnis zum Daueraufenthalt-EU,
- a Blaue Karte EU, ICT-Karte or Mobiler-ICT-Karte,
- a residence permit that allows employment for at least six months.
The provision lists exceptions and further cases.

Under BEEG §1(8), the claim lapses if taxable income in the last completed assessment period before the birth was more than 175,000 euros. Where another person also meets the conditions, the two incomes are added together ("mehr als 175 000 Euro").

The application must be made in writing (BEEG §7(1)). Payment is made retroactively only for the last three Lebensmonate before the month in which the application is received. Earlier months are not paid.

The decision is made by your Elterngeldstelle. If you disagree with it, you can lodge an objection (Widerspruch) there in writing within one month of receiving the decision.
